newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Italy April CPI seen falling to 1.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Italy April CPI seen falling to 1.8 pct.

text.p: Italy's consumer price inflation is seen falling under the 2.0 percent level in April paving the way for a possibile official interest rate cut by the end of the month, a Reuter poll showed on Wednesday.
On Tuesday, Treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told parliament he expected April CPI to come in at 1.8 percent year-on-year from 2.2 percent in March, the lowest since 1969.
Analysts were divided on the inflation outlook over future months as some saw prices starting to pick up while others said CPI should remain subdued for the rest of the year.
The 15 analysts polled by Reuters saw April inflation on average rising 0.2 percent month on month and 1.8 percent year on year. In March, CPI rose 0.1 percent month on month.
Italy's 11 sample cities publish their CPI data on Monday and Tuesday. National statistics body Istat will issue final data on May 6.
Analysts said April CPI should benefit from the statistical comparison with the same month of 1996 when prices rose 0.6 percent monthly and 4.5 percent yearly.

"The only seasonal factor in April is the quarterly rent reviews which did not show a sharp rise. A fall in petrol pump prices should also have a positive effect," Rodolfo Dozio, analyst at Banca Commerciale Italiana, said.

"There is the scope for a fall in inflation until June when it could reach 1.6 percent, but further dips will become more difficult after that because in July 1996 CPI fell 0.2 percent monthly and in August it rose only 0.1 percent," Dozio added.

Martino Dolfini, analyst at Chase Manhattan Bank, agreed but saw a "strong trend in rent rises although consumer demand continues to be weak. I don't see any risks," he said. He saw CPI at end-June standing at 1.5 percent but then start rising while still remaining under a 2.0 percent average for 1997.

Paolo Casadio, economist at Credito Italiano, said April CPI could even come in under 1.8 percent. "If rent hikes were around 1.0 percent and the food sector continued to be subdued we could see year-on-year inflation at 1.7 percent," he said.

Casadio said inflation after June will start picking up but not significantly. "We will go from 1.6 percent to 2.0 percent, but on average we will be at 2.0 percent with the differential over German inflation less than 0.5 percent on a yearly basis."

Stefano Lelli of Banco di Sardegna noted that the clothing sector, which in April traditionally sees price rises because of the new season, should not weigh significantly this year due to continuing weak demand.

On the possibility of an official central bank rate cut, Dozio said: "the Bank of Italy will cut interest rates by the end of the month. Such high real rates do not make sense, the lira cross is going extremely well, it's an opportunity not to be missed," he said. The Bank's discount rate is 6.75 percent.

"With inflation at 1.8/1.9 percent, all factors justify a 50 basis point easing based on economic fundamentals. A small cut would be a very positive signal because it would allow the scope for a further reduction," Casadio of Credito Italiano said.

Francesco Giordano, analyst at CSFB, also saw scope for a 50 basis point cut after the CPI data. "But the room for cuts has got smaller, given the U.S. Fed rate rise and the slight pick-up in economic growth in Europe. This could be the last rate cut," he said.
